speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1963-64 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Winnipeg today the Canadian wheat board is announcing the final payment on wheat delivered to the board during the crop year 1963-64. Producers delivered a total of 563,875,208 bushels of wheat to the board in the 1963-64 crop year. This is the largest volume of wheat ever delivered by producers to the board in a single crop year. The amount of the final payment to be distributed to producers is approximately $272 million. This final payment is a record in the history of board operations.
This is not, I need hardly remind members of the house, a payment by the government of Canada; it represents the net returns of the Canadian wheat board in the marketing of western Canadian wheat for the 1963-64 crop year. Of the total payment approximately $18 million will be distributed to producers of Durum wheat.
The average final payment for wheat other than Durum is 48.725 cents per bushel, which is also a record. The average final payment for Durum wheat is 42.317 cents per bushel. These average payments compare with 40.181 cents per bushel for grades of wheat other than Durum, and 64.780 cents per bushel for Durum wheat delivered by producers in the 1962-63 crop year. The board will commence issuing final payment cheques to producers on March 8.
The final payment is being made on a grade basis, as prescribed in the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The rates of final payment for the principal grades of wheat are as follows:

This announcement by the wheat board speaks for itself, Mr. Speaker. On behalf of the government may I add our congratulations to all those concerned in the growing, handling, transportation and selling of the 1963 crop. It was a magnificent achievement from which all parts of Canada benefited enormously. Never before has so much wheat of such high quality been produced. Never before has so much wheat been , handled and moved and sold so quickly and at such high prices. In particular may I extend congratulations to the Canadian wheat board, who are entrusted by parliament with responsibility for the sale of the prairie wheat crop on behalf of western producers. The handling of the 1963 crop is not only another evidence of the soundness of the board system of marketing; it is a tribute to the competence of the board and its staff.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1963-64 CROP YEAR
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1963-64 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe all Canadians can join with the minister in congratulating the Canadian wheat board for the tremendous job done last year. I think the business interests in this country realize now that when the grain of Canada sells not only in great volume but at good prices the whole country benefits.
I think we received an indication of the average amount in an answer to a question posed by the hon. member for Melville last week, in which he asked for average prices during the year. The average price for No. 1 northern at Fort William was approximately $2.05 which would indicate, if considered in the light of the amount of grain that is handled through Vancouver and Churchill, that the average received for grain sold out of all our ports last year must have been $2.08 approximately. This would mean that over and above the $1.50 already paid to the farmers in initial payments there was 58 cents left over. In relation to the 58 cents, let me state that the final payment for No. 1 wheat averaged 46.9 cents. So the next question in our minds, Mr. Speaker, is when was the pool closed off; because apparently in the last few
days of pool operations the returns were decreased.
I am not going to quarrel with the minister in respect of the final payment because I know the technique used by the board in settling the amount of this payment. Generally speaking it can be assumed to be quite satisfactory, but I should like to ask hon. members to consider the feelings of the minister next year when he rises to announce the final payments on the 1964-65 pool.
Mr. Speaker, the pool was closed off early this year so the full impact of the tremendous drop in price would not be felt in respect of this final payment. I suggest to the minister that he should fully enjoy this moment, because the minister who is in charge of the Canadian wheat board next year will have to face up to the fact that because of the lack of action in protecting the Canadian wheat board, and in view of the political decisions made before a price war started, the announcement then will not be so pleasurable.
This announcement by the minister does not involve just a question of pleasure. In my mind I see farmer after farmer in western Canada, having undertaken obligations with regard to land, machinery and other things he wants on the basis of $2 wheat, now having to face up to the fact that next year's final payment will be a price of approximately 20 cents less per bushel. This works out to $200 drop for every 1,000 bushels the farmer sells.
I congratulate the minister and join with him in the pleasure of this announcement today, but he is living the life of Riley. He is enjoying the policies of the previous government-

speechtext: -that were instrumental in finding these new markets, that started these long term agreements and slowly worked up the price by 50 cents a bushel. maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1963-64 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement which has just been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce regarding the final price for the 1963-64 crop year will be welcomed by the wheat producers of Canada, I am sure. This happy situation results from a combination of two fortuitous circumstances, a good crop of high quality combined with a shortage of wheat in the world, particularly because of

poor crops in the Soviet union and in China, It is fortunate we were able to avail ourselves of this circumstance, and I am sure the government and members of the House of Commons generally are happy that the farmers are to have such a good return. The minister himself has pointed out, of course, that this is not a government gift to the farmers. This is merely the final payment from the money received by the wheat board, which has the task of selling the farmers' wheat.
However, Mr. Speaker, unfortunately we cannot look to the present crop year with the same optimism. The president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool said recently, I believe, that the decline in the price of wheat which has already taken place means a reduction in the farmers' income this year of some $50 million to $75 million.
The reports at hand now indicate there are very large surpluses of wheat in Argentina and Australia together with an increase in the wheat crop in the European common market countries and an increase in the crop of the Soviet union of some 500 million bushels. This will mean that the problem of selling wheat at a price that will give the farmers a reasonable return in this crop year is going to be considerably more difficult than it was in the past crop year. Therefore I do hope that the minister, in conjunction with the wheat board, is taking cognizance of the change in the world situation with regard to both price and markets.
I would hope that in the very near future the minister will take the very first opportunity that presents itself to place before the house the government's wheat marketing policy, in order that we may know what it is and in order that the farmers may have some assurance that the loss in farm income is not going to be too great in the present crop year.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1963-64 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party join with the minister and the spokesmen for the other parties in welcoming this announcement today. I am not going to repeat many of the things that have been said, but certainly everyone must realize that an injection of $272 million into the economy of the country through the producers of wheat in western Canada is going to be beneficial to all Canadians no matter where they live. We are very happy to receive the news that this is the highest payment on record. We had some indications a few days ago that this was going to be so,
Grain Payments
and now that the final payment has been confirmed at an average of 48.75 cents we know it is not only the highest such payment per bushel but also the highest total payment in Canadian history.
We are apprehensive about the future, Mr. Speaker, because it is no secret that there has been some decline in the international wheat market recently. I know the minister has expressed concern about this very matter. I hope they are successful in negotiating with the other partners to the international wheat agreement so the situation will not deteriorate to the point where there will be open warfare, and that some kind of agreement can be reached to perhaps get the price back where it was.
Another thing that happened during the selling of wheat during the last crop year was that some 30 million bushels extra were milled into flour before being exported from Canada. This in fact provided a 24 hour, 7 day week production for all the flour mills in Canada. I should like to congratulate the minister especially, or the wheat board, or whoever was responsible for getting this amount of flour into the total volume of wheat during that period, because it was certainly a boon to the flour milling industry.
To be fair, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that wheat prices had declined something like 20 cents a bushel on the average but this, of course, is simply not true. This is the extreme. The average is perhaps down somewhere between 12 cents and 15 cents, or at about the same level it was before this large sale to the Soviet union. He suggested also that the pool had been closed early so it would not reflect some of the declines of recent days. This also is not the exact truth. I believe the wheat pool for the 1963-64 crop year was closed at approximately the same date as it was a year ago.
At a time when every Canadian in the country should have welcomed this announcement and given credit where it belongs, I had hoped that for once the previous minister of agriculture could have given the credit to those to whom it belonged. As I say, all through those years his government was in office they attempted to transfer credit for any grain sales to the policies of the government; in fact we know that he held up the announcement of the sale to red China for three days so he could get over there and make the announcement. Apparently, Mr. Speaker, we are never going to get that degree of modesty for which I was hoping on this auspicious occasion.

Grain Payments
We certainly welcome this announcement. We in this party give full credit where the credit belongs, and that is to the Canadian wheat board and all those other agencies who so effectively delivered the grain on time so that we had a completely satisfactory marketing year.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FINAL PAYMENT FOR 1963-64 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one has but to listen to the comments of the leaders of the two main parties in this house to realize what can happen when one of them is in office and the other in the opposition.
We are proud of the success achieved by western farmers in their wheat production for 1963-64. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is certainly to be congratulated for the splendid job he has done in the sale of our wheat. Our congratulations should also go especially to the Canadian wheat board, an agency which is mainly responsible for the success of our western farmers.
I hope with all my heart that my province can finally have such a body, which could be called the Canadian farm products board or by any other name. But we would be glad if there were such a board in the province of Quebec. It would then be in a position to deal with the Minister of Trade and Commerce in order to sell our products.
Following the announcement made a little earlier, I realize that it is essential for a province to have such an agency to obtain a reasonable price for its products.
The minister told us that Canada has never known such an era of prosperity. It is necessary of course to restrain the minister and the opposition feels that he goes too far. We, in the province of Quebec, did not benefit from that prosperity to a great extent, especially if we consider the prices now paid for feed grain. If that abundance of wheat had resulted in somewhat lower prices for feed grain in Quebec, I would agree that our province would have felt some measure of prosperity; but no, that abundance of wheat has no influence on prices in the province of Quebec.
The statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes me feel very happy for our western people. But here again I am not prepared to believe that the minister alone is responsible for the bumper crop of the western provinces in 1963-64. I will never believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has come to the point where he thinks he is the good Lord himself.

Such bountiful crop is due, in the first place, to perfect weather conditions, the work of the farmers, and also of the Canadian wheat board; it is the combination of these factors which has resulted in that situation and made it possible to take advantage of that wonderful opportunity for the marketing of our wheat, in short, the year just had to be favourable.
I come to the conclusion that the successful crop in the west was simply caused by wonderful weather conditions.
What would happen should a disaster occur in 1965? The westerners have had such an experience in the past.
Consequently, I ask the minister to stop making announcements of this kind; besides, he should bring out the true facts and, above all, think not only in terms of wheat, but also in terms of everything that is produced in each province of Canada.

subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Under the new rule as accepted by the house for this session, the Speaker is entitled to ask any hon. member to explain why there is special urgency, and at this time I would call upon the hon. member to do so.

subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the rules of the house I am not permitted to present any argument, but I do wish to apply myself to the matter of urgency respecting the subject matter of this motion. As the motion points out, the Steel Company of Canada has announced an increase in the price of steel of some 4 per cent, increasing steel prices by some $5 to $7 per ton, depending on grade. Other steel companies have announced that it is their intention to follow suit.
I would argue that it is most urgent that this matter be dealt with immediately and that opportunity for debate should be given this afternoon, because in my opinion a rise in steel prices will set off a chain reaction that will result in a very substantial increase in the cost of living. The increase in the price of steel will reflect itself in the cost of cars, trucks, tractors, farm implements, appliances such as washing machines and refrigerators, building materials, machines, machine tools. All these will be affected. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, eventually every housewife in Canada will feel the impact of this increase. This will affect the budgets of municipalities, provincial governments and departments of the federal government; therefore it will reflect itself in increased taxes all across this country. People who are desirous of building homes, office buildings,

Increase in Steel Price factories, will all feel the effect of an increase in the price of structural steel and building rod.
This concern is shared by many people. Yesterday the national farmers union, in presenting their brief to the federal government, drew attention to this fact. They said:
We express our concern at the announcement on February 23, 1965, by the Steel Company of Canada Limited that it intends to increase the prices of bar mill products from $5 to $7 a ton.
They went on to point out that the inflationary implications in the rise of basic steel products are certain to have widespread repercussions.
They pointed out that they are particularly concerned about the effect this will have upon farm machinery, Upon repairs for that machinery, and the wide range of equipment which is required on the average farm. They also point out in their brief that they see no justification for this increase; and they gave to the government of Canada, on the second page of their brief, a summary of the steady rise in profits which the steel companies have enjoyed right from 1956 up to the present time.
My second reason, Mr. Speaker, for stressing the urgency of having a discussion of this matter at once is that it is urgent that the public have all the facts as to whether this price increase is justified. This has been called in question by a number of people. Last week the Prime Minister told the house that he had received a wire from Mr. William Mahoney, the Canadian director of the united steelworkers of Canada, in which Mr. Mahoney pointed out that in his opinion there was no justification whatsoever for this increase. He pointed out that the Steel Company of Canada had increased its profits from some $21,158,000 in 1957 to $43,630,000 in 1964. Mr. Mahoney felt that the government should take immediate action to suspend any increase in price until the matter had been investigated with a view to seeing whether these increases were justified.
Last Friday, Mr. Claude Jodoin, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, wrote the Prime Minister-I have a copy of the letter here-which he again asked the Prime Minister to take steps to suspend this increase in price until the whole justification for it had been investigated. He pointed out to the Prime Minister that the Prime Minister's statement in the house, to the effect that there had been no recent increases in price, was completely unsound and that there have

been adjustments which have had the effect of pushing up the price of steel.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraith (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could raise a point of order. It seems to me that the hon. member is arguing in justification of his motion and is not addressing himself to the point which is before the house, namely the urgency of debate. I would ask that his argument be confined to that point.

subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am entirely in your hands, but I am trying to confine myself to the matter of urgency. I would prefer to accept your judgment on the matter rather than that of the President of the Privy Council, who may be somewhat sensitive on this subject. I was pointing out that here are the national farmers union, the head of the steelworkers union and the president of the Canadian Labour Congress who have all expressed their concern. This surely underlines the urgency of debate, in order that this matter may be discussed at once. I point out that both Mr. Mahoney and Mr. Jodoin are members of the Canada economic council, whose recent report states that one of our objectives for the next five years is to keep some price stability. The action of the Steel Company of Canada in raising their prices by 4 per cent is destroying that stability and is setting in motion a chain reaction that could bring about further inflation and further increases in the cost of living.
There are two other points I want to make, Mr. Speaker. The first, very briefly, is that the people of Canada have a right to know who is responsible for this increase in the cost of living. I think it is urgent that the people know this. The companies have tried to give the impression that this is due to increased wages. In his wire to the Prime Minister, Mr. Mahoney pointed out that today the labour cost in a ton of steel is actually $5.36 less than it was in 1957. We think the public have a right to know who is guilty, who is responsible for this unjustified increase in price which can have such an inflationary effect upon our economy.

subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Is this more important than the Canada pension plan?

subtopic: INCREASE IN STEEL PRICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member asks whether this is more important than the Canada pension plan. There is plenty of time to dispose of the Canada pension plan, but if steps are not taken by the government to stop this

spiral of inflation it will take away all the gains that the consumers of this country hope to get from the Canada pension plan.
The final reason for urgency, Mr. Speaker, is that I submit to Your Honour there is no other opportunity in this session for discussing this very important matter. There are no supply motions left. There are no departmental estimates on which this question can be raised. Therefore there is no opportunity available to the members of the house to discuss this matter, and there is no opportunity for the government to tell parliament and the people of Canada what they intend to do. We say that action now is vital, that any further delay would be fatal. We say that the government must act, and act in the next few days, or the repercussions from this increase in the price of steel will be reflected throughout our entire economy.
I point out that faced with a similar situation a few years ago the late President Kennedy acted, and acted promptly, and he received the support of the American people in so doing. We say the time has come to discuss this matter, so the government of Canada can tell the people of this country what action it intends to take under these serious circumstances.

speechtext:
The motion is also out of order on the basis that it is the type of motion which contemplates legislation. Under the practice here, that type of motion cannot be made under standing order 26. In support of that argument I refer Your Honour to citation 100(8), which appears at page 91 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, where reference is made to the British rule. I shall only read the relevant part, although the whole paragraph is applicable. The Speaker said:
I do not think that, under the standing order of 1882, a motion on a subject of this kind, having such a very wide scope, was ever contemplated. What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs. But I do not think it was contemplated-if the house will allow me to state my views-that a question of very wide scope, which would demand legislation to deal with it in any effective manner, should be the subject of discussion on a motion for the adjournment of the house, because, if that was so, we might have repeated motions made by the opposition of the day, not so much in the direction of censuring the government for action which had been taken or not taken, for bringing to notice some grievance demanding instant remedy, as in the direction of wishing to introduce legislation on some particular subject.
Then he went on to say that is not the purpose of the standing order.
It is not a question of the importance of the subject matter, which I think was acknowledged by the Minister of Finance the other day. It is the fact that the hon. member has no right to use standing order 26 in the way in which he contemplates using it; because he is seeking to demand or invite legislation by the government, whereas standing order 26 was never intended for that purpose. As has been pointed out by many hon. members, there is no doubt that this is an important matter, but that is not the position in which the Chair finds itself. As I said yesterday, what the Speaker has to decide is whether there is a prima facie case. As pointed out in Beauchesne's parliamentary rules, fourth edition, citation 100, paragraph 3, "urgency" within rule 26 does not apply to the matter itself but means urgency of debate. As I also suggested yesterday, the matter should be so pressing that public interest would suffer if it was not given immediate action. This principle is, of course, drawn from Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 100 again, paragraph 2.
Citation 100, paragraph 8 of Beauchesne's fourth edition states:
What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs.
Perhaps I should stress at this time those two words "sudden emergency". Is the matter which has been proposed for discussion something which occurred so suddenly that it is in the nature of a national emergency, almost in the category of a catastrophe, which has taken place very quickly? Has it occurred so recently or so suddenly that the important business now before the house should be set aside to discuss it, and in this case the subject is the increase in steel prices? Yesterday I said:
It seems to me that any such sudden emergency should be sufficient to justify the setting aside of the important business of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with a question asked me last Friday by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle as to Canada's intentions with regard to the serious wheat shortage in India. In reply I should like to point out that last fall the government announced that Canadian wheat valued at $7 million would be shipped to India under our normal Colombo plan procedures. This was done last autumn. The government also indicated at that time that the wheat situation would be kept under review to determine what, if anything, further Canada could do to help.
Because of the United States dock strike, shipments of the United States wheat contribution to India this year have been delayed and as a consequence particularly serious wheat shortages have developed in India and are likely to be critical over the next few months. India has therefore been seeking on an urgent basis alternate sources of supplies.
To help with this situation the Canadian government, in addition to the wheat grant mentioned above, has now decided to make a further grant of 100,000 tons of wheat. The shipment of this new gift will begin about mid-March and will go from Atlantic ports.


About one half of the amount involved will be Ontario wheat, with the remainder coming from western Canadian production. The total cost will be approximately $7 million, and a supplementary appropriation in this amount will be sought in the current fiscal year. I am sure the house will approve of this gift to India.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question
Inquiries of the Ministry to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in his capacity as superintendent general of Indian affairs. This great man lived two lives, first in the old customs in which he was trained.
Then, when these were outlawed, instead of putting on a grim face, he learned a new way of life.

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: TRIBUTE ON DEATH OF CHIEF OF KWAKIUTL NATION

-and met the challenge of the world.
That's why Chief Billy lived so long.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue.
Yesterday the minister told us that if arrangements were made between the province of Quebec and the federal government, federal civil servants in the province of Quebec would contribute to the Quebec pension plan while if arrangements were not made between the two governments, those civil servants would have to contribute to the federal government plan.
A little later the Minister of National Revenue stated that Quebec members of parliament would be considered as being from Ontario and would therefore contribute to the federal pension plan.
Would the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) tell us if it would not be advisable to include in the same category as federal civil servants the Quebec members of parliament who would be able to contribute immediately to the provincial government pension plan?

Canada Pension Plan

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I mentioned yesterday, if there is an agreement reached under clause 4 of the bill a federal civil servant in the province of Quebec will contribute to the Quebec pension plan. Ottawa is where members of parliament obtain their remuneration and do their work. Under the bill a member of parliament is treated as an employee in Ottawa and would contribute to the Canada pension plan.
However, I do not think that this is a very important matter for a member of parliament in the long run, because if there is an exactly similar pension plan to the Canada pension plan in the province of Quebec, then supposing a member of parliament spent his time here for a number of years and then went back to Quebec, the benefits which he would ultimately receive would be from the Quebec plan, and there is a financial arrangement whereby the Canada pension plan would make a reimbursement. Similarly if a civil servant stationed in Ottawa went to Quebec to work, then if such an agreement was entered into under clause 4 he would contribute to the Quebec pension plan. Then if he came back to spend the last few years of his contributory period in Ontario or to retire in Ontario, he would receive his payment entirely from the Canada pension plan, there being an arrangement for reimbursement back and forth so that a person gets one cheque only. So it really would not make any difference in the long run.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Chairman.
The Minister of National Revenue always uses the conditional when referring to clause 4 or to that agreement between the province of Quebec and the federal government. Could the minister tell us if, at present, he believes such an agreement will be reached between the two governments or what are the odds that it will not come about?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would say that there would be such agreement, but one must speak in conditional terms. First of all, we have not yet got a Canada pension plan because this legislation has not been passed. The province of Quebec has not got a pension plan either because it has not been approved yet by the legislature of the province of Quebec. So you must speak in conditional terms and say "if" such an agreement is

made. But I can assure my hon. friend that consequent upon the legislation being passed and a plan in substantially similar terms coming into effect, such an agreement will in all probability be made.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Just supplementary to that, I take it that in any pension plan, either the Canada pension plan or a provincial pension plan, the portability sections will cover all that we have just been speaking about?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I take the minister to be even more correct about the conditional aspect of this than he was. He said that he felt quite sure that an agreement would be entered into, and I agree with him that such an agreement will most likely be entered into. But I think the minister should have gone one step further and said that that agreement will be effective, so to speak, only as long as Quebec does not in the future change its own plan, which of course it has the constitutional right to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I think that is quite true. The interchange of benefits between the two plans continues into the future only if the Canada pension plan is not changed and the Quebec pension plan stays as it is. They must keep in step or else there is not the portability which my hon. friend has mentioned before.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I think we all hope that there will be complete portability, but the economic conditions of any province which has opted out could be such as to require the government of the day in that province substantially to change its plan. If that happened there would be serious consequences as far as portability is concerned, but these serious consequences might not be as important a consideration as the economic conditions which prompted the change. I do not think we should kid ourselves that we have a national plan under all circumstances.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: I think we can say that in light of the present intentions indicated by the resolution which is before the Quebec legislature and the bill which is before this House of Commons we will have a portable plan, a national plan, at this point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: True, at this point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
One cannot foresee what will happen in the future as years go by, but one would assume that for the benefit of both parties-and there are benefits for both sides in keeping the plans similar-it is likely that the plans would continue to be very similar

in nature, and in effect we would have a national plan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will this house be able to see the Quebec plan before we are asked to pass the Canada pension plan?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, referring to clause 103 which deals with numbers to be assigned under Bill No. C-136, I remember that yesterday a question was asked about this matter after the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) asked what departments would have access to those files. It was stated that four departments would have access to them, namely: the Department of Labour, as concerns the numbers, the Department of National Revenue, as concerns the collection of income taxes, the Department of Finance, as concerns administration, and the Department of
Canada Pension Plan
National Health and Welfare, as concerns the payment of benefits.
I would like to draw the attention of my colleagues to the fact that Quebec will have a parallel system; therefore, those files will be open to three or four federal departments, which means five, six or seven departments, since the same files which are used by the federal departments would, under the so-called agreements-and I use the conditional -be open to Quebec officials as well as Ottawa officials.
What is our position? We must carry a number under Bill No. C-136, and we just learned that a pension plan similar to the one contained in Bill No. C-136 was introduced in the Quebec legislature in January. Furthermore, as I pointed out, we do not have the French version of the report dealing with the study made by the committee where some of us brought forth our suggestions. We do not know, either, what went on at the meetings which preceded those agreements, under co-operative federalism, as regards this bill. We know nothing about that.
That is why we are inclined to think in the province of Quebec, and rightly so, that co-operative federalism is nothing but disguised hypocrisy brought to a legislative system. We ask direct questions but we receive no answer. I can understand the minister being anxious to have this bill passed; after all, it is the plan drafted by the provincial technocrats, the Quebec socialists, which Ottawa is putting into law now, according to the information we got yesterday.
This is my question. Those who drafted Bill No. C-136 and who will look after the administration of the act have recognized that four departments will have access to these records. I would like to know whether they will give access to the records to others than to officials of the federal departments of national health and welfare, labour, national revenue and finance.

Canada Pension Plan
general subject when we are considering the appropriate clause, which is subsequent to the one now under discussion.

parently there were many duplications and there was a necessity for periodic re-issues of booklets and re-assignations of numbers.

It is our intention that this system will be maintained in the future. This was found to be necessary in respect of members of the insured labour force and, furthermore, it is very expensive. A great deal of advertising is required in order that individuals will realize that a pension plan cannot be operated efficiently without a numbering system. In order to save time and money the social insurance numbering system was instituted last year replacing the unemployment insurance numbers. In this manner it will serve a dual purpose, if as and when the Canada pension plan is adopted.
These numbers will be available first of all to the unemployment insurance commission, and second to the Canada pension plan administration: I refer of course to the numbers already issued on a compulsory or voluntary basis. It is our intention that this numbering system will continue on into the future so that, as was pointed out last night by my colleague, if an individual moves from Perth to Quebec city he will continue to have the same number. If an agreement is in force, he would have a number under the Canada pension plan and he would continue to bear this number when he went into the Quebec pension plan. I may say that all information about an individual contributor or beneficiary which is obtained in the course of the administration of the act must be treated confidentially as set forth in subsection (1) of this section. Persons in the employ of the crown may not provide that information to other people or give others access to that information except in those cases specifically spelled out in the remaining subsections.
The first exception is indicated in subsection (2). This provides that a contributor or beneficiary, or his agent, may authorize the minister to divulge information about his earnings record or pension entitlement to some third person whom he names in his written request. In this way an employer will be able to obtain the necessary information about his employee or former employee to make it possible for him to integrate any benefits that are payable under a private pension plan with those payable under the Canada pension plan.
Subsection (3) provides that information obtained by an employee of the Department of National Health and Welfare in the course of administering this act can only be made

available to employees of the other departments named when it is necessary that this be done for the purposes of administration of the act. For example (a) national revenue employees may have to be notified that an individual contributor has applied for and been granted a pension and therefore is no longer required to contribute to the plan. National revenue employees would also have to be notified regarding failure of an employer to make contributions on behalf of an employee when this information has come to a local office of the Department of National Health and Welfare from the individual employee concerned.
And (b), Department of Finance employees in the office of the comptroller of the treasury will have to be notified that the payment of a benefit in a specified amount has been approved and authorized by the minister in order for the comptroller of the treasury to issue the pension cheque.
And (c), unemployment insurance commission officers will have to be notified when individual employees or self-employed people apply to the Department of National Health and Welfare for the issuance of a social insurance number. The application form for such a number will have to be passed to the unemployment insurance commission for checking against the master index to see if a number has already been issued to the individual concerned.
And (d), the chief actuary of the department of insurance is required by the act to conduct a review of the operations of the plan every five years; for such actuarial analyses he will naturally need data concerning contributions to and benefits paid out from the plan. The advisory committee will need to have both actuarial and statistical studies conducted in reviewing the operations of this act. The research and statistics division of this department will be carrying on special studies on the operations of the plan and may seek the co-operation of the dominion bureau of statistics in the conduct of some of these studies. Some information in connection with these studies will have to be passed to officers of the dominion bureau of statistics; but it is well known that the dominion bureau of statistics employees must observe the strictest secrecy in the handling of all information which they receive.
Subsection (4) provides that information about individual contributors or beneficiaries which is obtained by employees of the Department of National Revenue, the unemployment insurance commission or the Depart-20220-753
Canada Pension Plan
ment of Finance may be provided to officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the other departments concerned with the administration of the act. This does not mean that all the confidential information contained on an income tax return is going to be made available to officers of other departments. There will be no need for the officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare to have any information about an individual's tax exemptions, or his marital status, or the number of businesses which he conducts, or the bankruptcy of his business, or the size of his profits; none of these data are pertinent to this act. What the act does require is that information about an employee's or a self-employed person's pensionable earnings in a year up to $5,000, and contributions to the plan, be passed to the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Finance and the department of insurance in order for the act to be properly administered. This provision is necessary because the information will be forthcoming from the T-4 slips and the T-l general returns under the Income Tax Act, and the information on these forms is, of course, normally restricted to the authorized officials of the Department of National Revenue. Information about individual self-employed persons may have to be passed by the Department of National Revenue to the unemployment insurance commission in cases where the self-employed person has not yet been assigned a social insurance number. It should be borne in mind that the administration of this act will be carried out in part by the Department of National Revenue, in part by the Department of National Health and Welfare, in part by the office of the comptroller of the treasury and in part by the unemployment insurance commission. Each of these departments must be free to pass any necessary information to the appropriate officers of the other departments in order that they may carry out their responsibilities in connection with the administration of this act.
For example, any information about the numbering system will involve the unemployment insurance commission, and any information about the payment or non-payment of pension benefits will involve the office of the comptroller of the treasury. This is particularly so until the time when the Department of National Health and Welfare obtains its own computer.
Subparagraph (b) of subsection (4) provides that, where social insurance numbers have

been assigned to people under any other act of parliament, information about these numbers and the applications for such numbers may be passed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Since people may apply for numbers through the unemployment insurance offices or through the Department of National Health and Welfare offices, or in effect through the Department of National Revenue in the case of a self-employed person who submits a contribution without first having obtained a social insurance number, provision must be made for the information contained in the application form to be passed to the agency that is charged with maintaining the master index of social insurance numbers, namely the unemployment insurance commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I came into office, when the member for Perth was the minister, the associations in this country which represent the former nationals of West Germany had been in touch with the department requesting the government of Canada to negotiate with the government of West Germany, because of peculiar provisions in their legislation to the effect that anyone who contributed to the pension plan in West Germany, and who emigrated from Germany to Canada and became a Canadian citizen, lost any claim to benefits. At about the time I took office, or shortly after, in August of 1963, I had discussions with the minister of labour for West Germany regarding this situation. Those discussions were subsequently followed up through the Department of External Affairs.
As I explained earlier this afternoon, one of the difficulties we face in respect of these reciprocal agreements arises because we base our legislation on flat rate pensions, quite unlike the earnings related basis of the West German pension scheme which was negotiated by Bismarck, and was the first pension scheme to be established in the western world. For this reason it is virtually impossible to integrate them.
During that same time when I was abroad I had discussions with the then minister of finance for the United Kingdom regarding the meshing of, or reciprocal agreements for, United Kingdom legislation and any potential Canadian legislation. This has been the subject of an exchange of correspondence over a lengthy period of time. The difficulty involved is that one cannot initiate detailed discussions-and they have to be detailed because these are very complicated plans and require a great deal of discussion before they can be integrated-until legislation is enacted. The idea is not that we should have part of one plan and part of another plan, but that participants should receive benefits from either one or the other depending upon where the individuals spend most of their productive lives and make the greater portion of their contributions. Until such legislation is enacted it really is not possible to go into these negotiations, except in a very general way. It is possible to obtain, as I just indicated we

have obtained, general expressions of approval and desire.

maintopic: GRAIN-WHEAT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FINAL PAYMENTS FROM 1958
GRAIN-WHEAT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FINAL PAYMENTS FROM 1958
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day I asked a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) regarding the final payments that had been made by the Canadian wheat board on the 1958 wheat crop, and up until this year. I asked this question because of the comments that were made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) after the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced the final payment on the 1963 crop. I was disappointed when, instead of welcoming the most gratifying results that had been announced by our minister, he chose to take advantage of the occasion to make a partisan speech. In brief he was saying that when he and his government were in office, results were much better.

maintopic: GRAIN-WHEAT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FINAL PAYMENTS FROM 1958
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: GRAIN-WHEAT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FINAL PAYMENTS FROM 1958
speechtext:
Here I should like to comment upon an editorial which I saw in a newspaper, the Western Producer for February 25, printed in Saskatoon. This editorial says, in part:
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
For Messrs. Alvin Hamilton, John Diefenbaker and others to suggest that if they had been in power things would have been different is the worst kind of misleading drivel. At no time in the Diefenbaker regime did the government face up to the situation with regard to wheat marketing as it now prevails.
With this in mind I thought that the house should know how much the Canadian wheat board have paid in the years when the Conservative government was in power.
I must admit that it still surprises me that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle could continue to think that he personally was responsible when he was minister of agriculture for the selling of our wheat, when he knows as well as we all do that the wheat board is given the responsibility for marketing prairie wheat. I have yet to hear the former minister -and I am sorry he is not here tonight- give credit where credit is due. Instead he seems to be going about the west making statements to undermine the wheat board. He says that there is a price war between the United States and Canada, and I think that this is very damaging to the wheat board's position. He knows that the wheat board, as I have said, is responsible for selling our Canadian wheat, but I have yet to hear him give credit where credit is due. I admire the straightforward attitude that is taken by our minister in the present government.

maintopic: GRAIN-WHEAT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FINAL PAYMENTS FROM 1958
speechtext: Ask the farmers about it; they know.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: GRAIN-WHEAT-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FINAL PAYMENTS FROM 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question put to me by the hon. lady was: What were the final payments made by the Canadian wheat board for 1958 and subsequent crops? I have the figures here. In the crop year 1958-59 the average final payment was 9.2 cents per bushel. In 1959-60 it was 12 cents a bushel, and in 1960-61, 31.8 cents a bushel. The figure for 1961-1962 is for spring wheats excluding Durums and the reason I switch here is because of the peculiar position of prices in that year for Durums which made the average a little different. Therefore I switch over to a comparable position with the statement I made in the house today. In 1961-62 the average payment was 43 cents. In 1962-63 it was 40.2 cents; and today, as I announced, the wheat board paid an average of 48.7 cents.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.12 p.m.
